body.p: enables you to install and execute unmodified versions of macOS and Mac OS X guests on supported host hardware. This feature is experimental and thus unsupported.
Be aware of the following important issues before you try to install a macOS guest:

li.p: macOS is commercial, licensed software and contains both license and technical restrictions that limit its use to certain hardware and usage scenarios. You must understand and comply with these restrictions.
In particular, Apple prohibits the installation of most versions of macOS on non-Apple hardware.

These license restrictions are also enforced on a technical level. macOS verifies that it is running on Apple hardware. Most DVDs that accompany Apple hardware check for the exact model. These restrictions are not circumvented by and continue to apply.

Only CPUs that are known and tested by Apple are supported. As a result, if your Intel CPU is newer than the macOS build, or if you have a non-Intel CPU, you will likely encounter a panic during bootup with an Unsupported CPU exception.
Ensure that you use the macOS DVD that comes with your Apple hardware.

The macOS installer expects the hard disk to be partitioned. So, the installer will not offer a partition selection to you. Before you can install the software successfully, start the Disk Utility from the Tools menu and partition the hard disk. Close the Disk Utility and proceed with the installation.

body.p:
Limitations
The graphics resolution currently defaults to 1024x768 as macOS falls back to the built-in EFI display support. See Video Modes in EFI for more information on how to change EFI video modes.
Depending on your system and version of macOS, you might experience guest hangs after some time. This can be fixed by turning off energy saving. Set the timeout to Never in the system preferences.
By default, the EFI enables debug output of the macOS kernel to help you diagnose boot problems. Note that there is a lot of output and not all errors are fatal. They would also show when using a physical Apple computer. You can turn off these messages by using the following command: $ VBoxManage setextradata VM-name "VBoxInternal2/EfiBootArgs" " "
To revert to the previous behavior, use the following command: $ VBoxManage setextradata VM-name "VBoxInternal2/EfiBootArgs" ""
It is currently not possible to start a macOS guest in safe mode by specifying the -x option in VBoxInternal2/EfiBootArgs extradata.

section.title: macOS 10.14 and Later Guests
section.p: There are separate guest OS types for macOS 10.14 Mojave, 10.15 Catalina, 11 Big Sur, 12 Monterey, 13 Ventura, 14 Sonoma, 15 Sequoia and 26 Tahoe (Intel versions only). Select the type matching the macOS release you install. In addition to the recommended hardware settings (EFI firmware, ICH9 chipset, I/O APIC, HPET, AHCI storage, Intel PRO/1000 MT Server network adapter, HD Audio, USB 3.0 controller with USB tablet and keyboard), VMs of these types differ from the older Mac OS X types as follows:

li.p: The DMI (SMBIOS) tables describe a Mac model supported by the selected release instead of the host system: iMac18,3 for macOS 10.14, iMac19,1 for macOS 10.15 up to 15 and iMac20,1 for macOS 26. The serial numbers are not changed. To use the host information like the older types do, set the VBoxInternal/Devices/efi/0/Config/DmiUseHostInfo extra data value to 1, or to 0 for the generic values. The individual values can be overridden as described in Configuring the BIOS DMI Information.

On Intel hosts with a CPU model which the macOS kernel does not know, for example Tiger Lake, Alder Lake and later CPUs, the CPU is presented to the guest as an Intel Coffee Lake CPU (family 6, model 0x9e), because the macOS kernel otherwise panics with Unsupported CPU. This is not done if a CPU profile other than host is selected. The presented family, model and stepping can be changed with the VBoxInternal/CPUM/MaxIntelFamilyModelStep extra data value, for example 0x00069E0D (stepping in the lowest byte, then model and family).
The EFI firmware reports APFS and large BaseSystem support to the guest.

section.p: macOS requires a device key which is stored in the System Management Controller (SMC) of Apple hardware. On Apple hosts reads it from the host. In all other cases it must be configured for the VM, otherwise macOS fails to decrypt protected system components and does not start its user interface. does not include this key. A warning is shown when a macOS VM is started without a key. Use the following command to set the 64 character key of the Apple hardware the guest is licensed to run on:

macOS 13 Ventura and later only run on CPUs with the instruction set extensions of the Intel Haswell generation (AVX2, BMI1, BMI2, FMA, MOVBE, LZCNT and others). If the virtual CPU lacks any of them, the guest fails to start with the message Library not loaded: /usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib. warns about this when the VM is started. Make sure hardware virtualization is used, keep the CPU profile at host and the CPUID portability level at 0.

li.p: Assign at least 4 GB of memory and 2 CPUs, for macOS 13 and later at least 8 GB and 4 CPUs.
Use a virtual hard disk of at least 80 GB (macOS 11 and later), with the AHCI (SATA) controller.
Keep the paravirtualization interface at Default, which selects the Minimal interface for macOS guests. macOS uses it to determine the TSC and bus frequencies.
Use the most recent installer of the respective macOS release.
